chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Sayf ibn 'Amira, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, who said:

I was with Abu Alqama, Al-Harith ibn al-Mughira, and Abu Hassan in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). Alqama had dyed [his beard] with henna, Al-Harith had dyed with woad (black dye), and Abu Hassan did not dye. Each of them said to him, 'What do you think of this? May Allah have mercy on you,' while gesturing towards his own beard. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'It is beautiful.' They said, 'Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) used to dye with woad?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Yes, that was when he married the Saqafiyya; her slave girls took him and dyed him.'

key_terms.الثَّقَفِيَّة: The Saqafiyya, a specific wife of Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him), known by this epithet.
key_terms.الْحِنَّاء: Henna, a reddish-brown dye plant commonly used for beard dyeing.
key_terms.الْوَسْمَة: Woad, a plant used to produce a black dye, often used to darken the beard.
key_terms.جَوَارِيهَا: Her slave girls, referring to the female servants in the household of the Imam.

ai.seo_question: What did the Imams say about dyeing the beard with henna or black dye (woad)?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the permissibility and aesthetic appreciation of grooming, specifically beard dyeing, within Shia tradition, distinguishing between the natural red of henna and the black of woad. It provides historical context by linking Imam al-Baqir’s practice to domestic life, illustrating that personal adornment was not merely ritualistic but also influenced by social and familial dynamics. The narration underscores the Imam’s approval of maintaining a dignified appearance, a theme often associated with following the Sunnah of the Prophet and the Imams.
